items.title: Export validates its own output
items.body:
`exportJobBackup` serializes the applications and then runs the result through `parseJobBackup` before returning it. The comment says why: never generate a backup the importer cannot restore. If the app's data somehow breaks the schema, the export **fails now**, on backup day, while the data still exists, instead of producing a file that is refused on restore day, when you need it most.

Why the others are wrong:
- **truncates to 2 MB**: nothing is truncated; an oversized export would simply fail.
- **warms caches**: the second pass is a check, not an optimisation.
- **concurrent edits**: serialization is synchronous; nothing can change the array mid-way.

excerpts.quote: const text = JSON.stringify({ format: FORMAT, version: 1, applications }, null, 2); parseJobBackup(text); // Never generate a backup the importer cannot restore.

items.title: A catch that swallows its own validator's error
items.body:
`new URL('javascript:alert(1)')` succeeds, so the allowlist check runs and calls `fail('URL must use http or https.')`. But `fail` **throws**, and that call sits inside the `try`. The `catch` right below catches it and calls `fail` again with the generic "URL must be an absolute http or https URL." So that is the message the user sees. The record is still rejected, so the safety rule holds, but the specific message can never appear. The lesson: wrap only the call that can throw, `new URL(...)`, in the `try`.

Why the others are wrong:
- **accepted**: it is rejected; only the message is wrong.
- **the specific message**: that is the tempting prediction the guide warns about; the catch replaces it.
- **not valid JSON**: that message comes from the `JSON.parse` catch, which is long past.

excerpts.quote: try { if (!['http:', 'https:'].includes(new URL(value.url).protocol)) fail('URL must use http or https.'); } catch { fail('URL must be an absolute http or https URL.');
a `try` should wrap only the call that can throw (`new URL(...)`), never the validation that follows it

items.title: Validate the whole array before writing anything
items.body:
`commitJobBackup` calls `parseJobBackup(text)` first and only then calls `storage.set`. `parseJobBackup` validates every record and throws at the first bad one. A throw means the `storage.set` line is never reached. So with one malformed record anywhere, **nothing changes** in storage; the old list stays. The tests check that `storage.set` was called zero times for every rejection.

Why the others are wrong:
- **clears the old data first**: there is no clear step; the only write is the final `set`.
- **earlier records saved**: records are not written one by one.
- **599 saved, one skipped**: the concepts chapter warns against quietly saving a convenient subset.

excerpts.quote: export async function commitJobBackup(storage, text) { const applications = parseJobBackup(text); await storage.set('jobtracker:data', JSON.stringify(applications));
Validation completes before persistence, so invalid row 500 cannot leave the first 499 rows saved.

items.title: Start here: a 64-line backup module
items.body:
Daybook (the `jobtrack` project) keeps a list of job applications in local storage. The course studies one feature: exporting the list as a JSON backup and importing a backup to replace it. The central skill, in the course's words, is runtime schemas, atomic imports and asynchronous write ordering.

The whole feature is one small file, `src/jobBackup.js`, with three functions: `parseJobBackup`, `exportJobBackup` and `commitJobBackup`. For each, note what it calls and in what order. Read it first, top to bottom. Then:

1. `astraupskill/02-CONCEPTS.md`: input boundaries, invariants, validation versus normalisation.
2. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md`: the implementation excerpt, how to reason through it, three variations to predict, and the tests.
3. `05-PRACTICE.md` and `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md`.

The course README warns that the test suite is slow; it suggests not running it in your inner loop. Many questions can be answered by reading the validator in program order.

excerpts.quote: This is a hands-on course for a junior software engineer using the actual project in `jobtrack`. The central skill is **runtime schemas, atomic imports and asynchronous write ordering**. The implementation is already present: use it as a worked example, then recreate a small variation independently.

readMore.why: The worked change, variations and tests.

items.title: Two bounds protect two different things
items.body:
The 2 MB file bound is checked before `JSON.parse` runs: it limits how much text the app is willing to **read and parse**. The per-field bound limits each value the app will **store and render** for a long time afterwards. They protect different resources. One record with a 1.9 MB notes field would pass the file bound easily, and then sit in storage and on screen forever.

Why the others are wrong:
- **the file bound is advisory**: it is enforced, at the first line of `parseJobBackup`.
- **keeps ids unique**: ids are checked with a `Set`, unrelated to size.
- **JSON escaping makes it unreliable**: the bound measures the real bytes with `TextEncoder`; reliability is not the issue.

excerpts.quote: new TextEncoder().encode(text).length > MAX_BACKUP_BYTES) throw new Error('Choose a JSON backup no larger than 2 MB.');
the file bound is about what you are willing to *read*; the field bound is about what you are willing to *store and render*.

items.title: The first failing check in program order wins
items.body:
For each record, the loop over all nine fields runs **first**, checking type and length. `role` is in that loop and is too long, so `fail('role must be bounded text.')` throws on the spot. The status check comes later, after the loop, and never runs. The validator reports only the first failure it meets, so the message is "Application 2: role must be bounded text."

Why the others are wrong:
- **errors combined**: `fail` throws immediately; nothing collects a second error.
- **expected an object**: the record is an object; that guard passes.
- **domain rules outrank type checks**: order in the code decides, and the type loop comes first.

excerpts.quote: for (const field of ['id', 'company', 'role', 'location', 'url', 'status', 'stack', 'date', 'notes']) {
if (!STATUSES.has(value.status)) fail('unknown status.');

items.title: A bare toThrow() accepts any error
items.body:
The rejection tests assert `rejects.toThrow()` with no message. That passes as long as **some** error is thrown, for whatever reason. The URL case was rejected (by the generic message), so the test passed, and nobody noticed that the specific "URL must use http or https." message could never appear. Asserting the exact message would have failed and revealed the swallowed branch. "Rejected for any reason" is a much weaker claim than "rejected for this reason".

Why the others are wrong:
- **Vitest cannot compare async messages**: `rejects.toThrow('...')` does compare messages; the tests just did not use it.
- **new URL was stubbed**: the tests call the real code.
- **URL cases were missing**: `{ url: "javascript:alert(1)" }` is in the parameterized list.

excerpts.quote: { url: "javascript:alert(1)" },
await expect(commitJobBackup(storage, text)).rejects.toThrow();
which is why the unreachable message was never noticed. A message-level assertion would have caught it.

items.title: The round trip rejects February 30
items.body:
The regex only checks the shape, and "2026-02-30" has the right shape. `new Date('2026-02-30T00:00:00Z')` does not fail either: JavaScript rolls the extra days into March, so the timestamp is a finite number. What catches it is the last part: `date.toISOString().slice(0, 10) !== value.date`. The date comes back as "2026-03-02", which differs from the input, so the record is rejected. (The guide says the date rolls to 1 March; since 2026 is not a leap year, it is actually 2 March. Either way it differs.)

Why the others are wrong:
- **Number.isFinite**: a rolled-over date is a valid timestamp, not NaN.
- **the regex knows month lengths**: it only checks digits and dashes.
- **accepted as typed**: the round trip rejects it.

excerpts.quote: date.toISOString().slice(0, 10) !== value.date) fail('date must be a real YYYY-MM-DD date or empty.');
A validator that only used `Number.isNaN(date.getTime())` would pass both.

items.title: A duplicate id rejects the whole file
items.body:
`parseJobBackup` keeps a `Set` of ids across all records. For the second record, `ids.has(value.id)` is true, so `fail('id is missing or duplicated.')` throws, with the record number in the message. Because `commitJobBackup` only writes after the whole array validates, nothing is stored: the **entire file** is rejected. The worked change states this as the policy: rejected as a whole, and the storage write must not be called.

Why the others are wrong:
- **last write wins**: there is no overwriting; validation throws first.
- **duplicate skipped**: the validator never skips records; it rejects the batch.
- **both import, UI dedupes**: nothing is imported at all.

excerpts.quote: if (!value.id.trim() || ids.has(value.id)) fail('id is missing or duplicated.');
A backup with a valid Acme application followed by another record with the same id is rejected as a whole. The storage set function must not be called.

items.title: Concept: describe correctness as invariants
items.body:
"The import works" is too vague to test. The concepts chapter asks for **invariants**: rules that must be true before and after an operation, phrased so you can observe them. "Editing preserves the record id" is one example.

The chapter's recipe: take each sentence of the feature's description and turn it into a small table with four columns: initial state, input, expected final state, expected feedback. Include at least one rejected input and one retry or repeat.

This is also how to read the tests. Each regression test arranges a starting state, acts by calling the real code, and asserts something observable, such as how many times the storage write was called. When a question asks "what ends up in storage?", the invariants are the answer key you should be able to write yourself.

excerpts.quote: An invariant is a rule that must remain true before and after an operation. “The app works” is too broad to test.
Turn each sentence into a small state table. The columns are initial state, input, expected final state and expected feedback.

items.title: Exactly 100,000 characters is accepted
items.body:
The length check is `item.length > (field === 'notes' ? 100000 : 5000)`. With a strict greater-than, 100,000 is not greater than 100,000, so it passes. Only 100,001 fails. The limit is **inclusive**. Probing the exact boundary value is the cheap test that documents this. And 100,000 characters is far below 2 MB, so the file-size limit does not interfere.

Why the others are wrong:
- **silently truncated**: the validator never changes a value; it accepts or rejects.
- **the 2 MB bound trips first**: 100,000 characters is roughly 100 KB.
- **greater-than-or-equal**: the code uses `>`.

excerpts.quote: if (typeof item !== 'string' || item.length > (field === 'notes' ? 100000 : 5000))
Now try the same payload with 100,000 characters exactly and confirm it is accepted - the comparison is `>`, so the limit is inclusive.

items.title: Atomic because it is one write
items.body:
There is no database transaction here, so atomicity has to come from somewhere else. The import replaces all applications with **one** call: `storage.set` of one serialized array under one key. A single write either happens or it does not; there is no half-written state in between. The concepts chapter adds that the storage host must honour that contract; client code alone cannot repair a host that writes and then wrongly reports failure.

Why the others are wrong:
- **a try block rolls back**: try/catch handles errors; it cannot undo a write.
- **await makes it atomic**: `await` only waits for the write to finish.
- **records written separately in a microtask**: they are not written separately at all.

excerpts.quote: await storage.set('jobtracker:data', JSON.stringify(applications));
Atomicity here is one key-value write: the browser shim uses localStorage.setItem.

items.title: Concept: a file is an input boundary
items.body:
Even a file the user exported themselves is untrusted input when it comes back in: it may have been edited, truncated or produced by an older version. `JSON.parse` only proves the text is valid JSON syntax, not that it means what you need. An array of numbers is valid JSON and is still not a list of applications.

So the importer checks in layers: the size of the text, whether it parses, the **envelope** (a format name, a version and an array of applications), limits, and then each record's fields and domain rules (id, company, status, date, URL).

Read `parseJobBackup` and number every check in the exact order it runs. For each one, note what it does when it fails (throw, skip, or default a value) and what message it produces. When two problems are present at once, your numbering tells you which one the user hears about.

excerpts.quote: A file is an input boundary, even when the user exported it from their own computer. JSON.parse proves syntax, not meaning: an array of numbers is valid JSON but is not an application list.
if (!backup || backup.format !== FORMAT || backup.version !== 1 || !Array.isArray(backup.applications)) throw new Error('Expected a Daybook applications backup, version 1.');

items.title: The record cap runs before any record is checked
items.body:
Right after the envelope check, `parseJobBackup` tests `backup.applications.length > 10000` and throws. That happens before the `map` that validates each record, so a backup of 10,001 is rejected **without** validating a single record. The point of the cap is to bound the validator's own work. Because the test is `>`, exactly 10,000 is still accepted.

Why the others are wrong:
- **at write time by the host**: the import never gets that far.
- **the cap is on bytes, not records**: the byte limit is a separate check; this one counts records.
- **after checking all records**: checking them all is what the cap exists to avoid.

excerpts.quote: if (backup.applications.length > 10000) throw new Error('A backup may contain at most 10,000 applications.');

items.title: Omitted fields default to empty strings
items.body:
The field loop reads each of nine fields as `record[field] ?? ''`. The `??` operator replaces `null` or `undefined` with the empty string, so a missing `location` or `notes` key becomes `''` before the type-and-length check runs, and `''` passes it. That line is the schema's answer to "which fields can be omitted?": all of them, except those a later rule demands (id, company, status). A **wrong type** is still rejected: `notes: 123` fails.

Why the others are wrong:
- **location is required**: no rule requires location; it may be empty.
- **imports undefined fields**: `??` turns them into empty strings, so no `undefined` is stored.
- **fails the envelope check**: the envelope only checks format, version and the applications array.

excerpts.quote: const item = record[field] ?? ''; if (typeof item !== 'string' || item.length > (field === 'notes' ? 100000 : 5000)) fail(`${field} must be bounded text.`); value[field] = item;
